text: Write rules the team can follow
After this you can outline a practical configuration management plan.

A configuration management plan is the agreed playbook for controlling a particular product. It identifies scope, roles, controlled items, reference versions, review authority, required records and verification methods. A useful plan is specific enough that two people would handle the same request consistently. The plan itself needs an owner and a revision history.

items: Define the product boundary and stages of work. You should see: Readers know which items and activities are covered. If not: Record exclusions rather than leaving them implicit.
Name the owners, reviewers and decision roles. You should see: There is a clear route for approvals and disputes. If not: Identify who has authority to resolve gaps.
Describe item, document, change and audit workflows. You should see: A newcomer can locate the next step. If not: Replace abstract statements with usable actions.
Specify records, review intervals and plan maintenance. You should see: The playbook can keep pace with the project. If not: Assign someone to monitor plan changes.
Inferred: A plan assigns software acceptance to an engineer. It assigns release-record checks to a technician.

text: Write the plan so the next person can follow it without asking its author.
No single outline fits every product; omit irrelevant details deliberately.

items: Copying a plan from another project unchanged Its approval roles and item boundaries may be wrong. Fix: Review every field against the actual project.
